poems:
Two o'clock.
The fluorescent tube over aisle six
has been failing for a year
and will fail for another.
The copier warms up for no one.
Somewhere a nurse writes 1402 and hangs a new bag.
School buses idle behind the transportation lot, engines running, nobody aboard, forty minutes early because the driver has nowhere better to be.

Things moved to Monday:
the dentist,
the transmission,
the apology.
The afternoon's first regret is usually lunch.
The vending machine drops the wrong bag and considers the matter closed.
You are not tired. You are 2:07 p.m.
A pallet jack parked crooked in the aisle, handle up.
Afternoon, n. The part of the day that has to be gotten through.
2:10. The second half of the workday has not technically started.
Somebody's grandmother is winning at solitaire on a hospital tray table.
Instructions for 2:12: stand, drink water, sit back down, do not check the score.
The dog has given up on the mail carrier and gone back to the rug.
By 2:14 the pen clicking is a personality.
A forklift beeps twice and a man in a safety vest waves it back like he is landing a plane.
Two dozen kindergarteners asleep on mats. One is not. He is planning something.
No, I said the fourteenth. The fourteenth.
A carton of chocolate milk sweating on a cafeteria table, straw still wrapped.
The IV pump chirps. The nurse silences it without looking, the way someone shuts a car door behind them.
2:20. Third period, or a rerun, depending on your life.
A man in a warehouse is standing up asleep, technically working.
The office fridge at 2:22: labeled yogurt, unlabeled yogurt, a jar of capers from a previous administration.

2:23. A kickball arcs over a fence
and becomes legend.
No good idea has ever come at 2:24.
The gas station espresso machine makes a sound like a small argument.
Half a sandwich in the fridge, the name in marker crossed out and written again.

2:27 p.m.
The bell has not rung.
The bell will ring.
Nothing else is settled.

2:28. A stapler borrowed at nine
begins its new life two desks down.
Two men look into an open hood. Neither of them touches anything.
Half past two. The day has stopped pretending it will be different.
A laundromat dryer turning one shoe.
The substitute has stopped taking attendance.
Rain, or the chance of rain, discussed at length by two men who do not work outdoors.
Four people in the pharmacy line, one of them arguing about a coupon.

2:35.
The afternoon has a floor to it,
flat and long,
and you are standing on it.
A bin of tennis balls, one escaped, resting against the fence.
The word nap goes unsaid across six adjacent desks.
The custodian mops in figure eights, backing out of the room he just cleaned.
2:39 p.m. Half the class is already facing the door.
Staging: what forty school buses do for an hour before anyone needs them.
A ceiling fan on the wrong setting, turning backward, moving nothing.
The email you have avoided since morning is still there, and now it has a reply.
Two women on a bench outside the dialysis center, not talking, which is the point.
A stack of folding chairs against a gym wall, one of them leaning off.
2:45. Ten more minutes of real work, then the mind starts packing.

The receptionist alphabetizes a stack
that was already alphabetized.
A janitor's cart in a hallway. Spray bottle, gloves, radio turned low.
You will not remember 2:48 p.m. That is what it is for.
The intercom clicks on, then off. Whatever it was has been reconsidered.
Ten to three, the waiting-room part of the hour.
A hard hat upside down on a truck dash, full of receipts.

2:52. A phone charges behind the lobby ficus,
its owner squatting nearby like a prospector.
The plan made at nine is down to two items, both of them emails.
A kid sent to the office is reading the fire evacuation map.
Backpacks already on. Five minutes of open rebellion.
The whole building leans toward the door.
Somewhere an infusion finishes and a machine says so, twice.
A parent in the pickup line puts the car in park and gives up on the podcast.

2:59. A yawn goes around the conference room
like a collection plate.
